title: Present Perfect
subtitle: Connect the past to now — experiences, changes, and unfinished time.
objectives: Form the present perfect (have/has + past participle)
Use it for life experiences, without saying exactly when
Use it for a recent action with a present result
Use already, yet, just, never, and ever correctly

content.intro: The present perfect is one of the trickiest tenses for Portuguese speakers, because Portuguese doesn't have a direct equivalent. It connects something from the past to the present moment.

rules.heading: a) Form
rules.body: have/has + past participle. I/you/we/they have finished. He/she/it has finished.

rules.heading: b) Life experience (no specific time)
rules.body:
• She has visited Paris three times. (at some point in her life, we don't say exactly when)
  • I have never eaten sushi.

rules.heading: c) Recent action, present result
rules.body:
• I have lost my keys. (result: I don't have them now)
  • They have just arrived. (very recently, relevant now)

rules.heading: d) Key signal words
rules.body: already (before now, often in affirmatives), yet (up to now, in negatives/questions), just (very recently), never/ever (at any point in life)

examples: She has visited Paris three times.
I have never been to Japan.

commonMistakes.wrong: I have visited Paris last year.
commonMistakes.why: "Last year" is a finished, specific time — that needs the simple past, not the present perfect.

commonMistakes.wrong: She has went to the store.
commonMistakes.right: She has gone to the store.
commonMistakes.why: The present perfect needs the past participle (gone), not the simple past form (went).
The main verb needs the past participle form after "have."
"Yet" is used in questions and negatives; "already" is more typical in affirmative statements.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct present perfect form.

items.explanation: Third person singular: has + past participle.
Third person singular needs "has," and the participle of "go/be" here is "been."

items.prompt: I ___ my phone. I can't find it anywhere.
items.explanation: A recent action with a present result — "have lost" fits the context.

items.incorrect: I have visited Paris last year.
items.explanation: A specific finished time (last year) needs the simple past.

items.incorrect: She has went to the store.
answer: She has gone to the store.
items.explanation: The present perfect needs the past participle, not the simple past form.
Irregular past participle: break → broken, not "broke."

summary: Use it for life experiences (no specific time) and recent actions with a present result.
Never use it with a specific past time word (yesterday, last year) — use the simple past instead.
Already/just fit affirmatives; yet fits questions and negatives; never/ever describe life experience.
